text: Exercise 1.1, Question 5: Check whether 6ⁿ can end with the digit 0 for any natural number n.

meta.reviewNote: Question checked against NCERT exercise page. The paired answer is stored separately and is hidden in practice mode.

text: No. Since 6ⁿ=2ⁿ×3ⁿ has no factor 5, it is not divisible by 10; a number ending in 0 must be divisible by 10.

text: Exercise 1.2, Question 1: Prove that √5 is irrational.

meta.subject: maths
meta.heading: Real Numbers — Exercise 1.2
meta.reviewNote: Exercise question and radical notation transcribed from rendered NCERT PDF p9; verified visually.

text: Assume √5=a/b in lowest terms with b≠0. Then a²=5b², so the prime-divisibility lemma gives 5|a. Write a=5c; substituting gives b²=5c², so 5|b. This contradicts that a and b are coprime. Therefore √5 is irrational.

meta.subject: maths
meta.heading: Real Numbers — Exercise 1.2 solution
meta.reviewNote: Solution derived using the prime-divisibility lemma and irrationality proofs on NCERT pp6–8; algebra and contradiction steps independently checked. Answer is hidden in practice mode.

text: Exercise 1.2, Question 2: Prove that 3+2√5 is irrational.

meta.subject: maths
meta.heading: Real Numbers — Exercise 1.2
meta.reviewNote: Exercise question and radical notation transcribed from rendered NCERT PDF p9; verified visually.

text: Suppose 3+2√5 were rational. Then subtracting 3 and dividing by 2 would make √5 rational, contradicting that √5 is irrational. Hence 3+2√5 is irrational.
